newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese police charge top bureaucrat with bribery.
newsitem.headline: Japanese police charge top bureaucrat with bribery.

text.p: Police arrested a former top bureaucrat on Wednesday on charges of taking a 60 million yen ($530,000) bribe from a business executive, a Tokyo police spokesman said.

Former Vice Health Minister Nobuharu Okamitsu was accused of taking the cash from Hiroshi Koyama, head of a firm which runs homes for the elderly, a spokesman for the Metropolitan Police Department said.

On November 19, Okamitsu resigned from his job as the top career bureaucrat in the Health Ministry after partially admitting media accusations that he took gifts from Koyama in the form of two luxury sedans.
Okamitsu has repeatedly denied taking cash from the business executive, however.
The bribery scandal came as an embarrassment for Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's new government, which pledged to carry out sweeping reforms of Japan's over-powerful bureaucracy.

In a speech to parliament last Friday following his re-election, Hashimoto said he was ashamed by the Health Ministry affair. His Liberal Democratic Party formed a minority government after general elections held on October 20.

Hashimoto was expected to face opposition grilling in parliament over the affair, especially as the Health Ministry submitted a bill requiring local governments to provide full health care for the extremely ill and elderly.

Besides the cash and rental of the cars, Okamitsu was also suspected of taking 30 million yen ($265,000) in a separate cash payment for work on his Tokyo apartment and a golf club membership worth 9.5 million yen ($84,000) from Koyama, according to media reports.

Koyama, who heads a firm which runs specialised homes for the elderly, was first arrested last month on a bribery charge unrelated to Okamitsu. He was re-arrested on Wednesday over his ties to Okamitsu, police said.
In return for Koyama's cash and gifts, police said they suspect Okamitsu helped Koyama's firm obtain 360 million yen ($3.18 million) in government subsidies to build the specialised homes.
Media reports said Koyama often boasted about his connections to Health Ministry bureaucrats, who have the power to decide who is granted subsidies.
The latest bribery affair follows other scandals at the Health Ministry, which has jurisdiction over the nation's lucrative medical and pharmaceutical industries and welfare institutions.
In October, a senior ministry official was arrested for criminal negligence over his suspected role in the spread of HIV among haemophiliacs through untreated blood products.
Some 1,800 Japanese haemophiliacs contracted HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, through use of the products.

The ministry has also been accused of incompetence in dealing with a food poisoning outbreak caused by the O-157 E. coli bacillus germ, which killed 11 people, mainly schoolchildren, and made 9,500 ill earlier this year. ($1=113 yen)
